kill_fact:
TWO independent kills, both verified against primary sources, and either alone ends the asymmetry.

KILL 1 -- the merger agreement contains an express ANTI-divestiture carve-out, which is the exact opposite of what the bull's central pillar assumes. I pulled the executed Agreement and Plan of Merger (Exhibit 2.1 to Cintas Form 8-K, filed 2026-03-11) and read Section 5.5 verbatim. Section 5.5(d): 'Notwithstanding anything in this Section 5.5 or anything else in this Agreement, neither Parent or any of its Affiliates shall be obligated to offer or agree to do any of the following (and neither the Company nor any of its Affiliates shall, or shall offer or agree to, do any of the following without Parent's prior written consent): (i) sell, divest or discontinue any portion of the assets, liabilities, activities, businesses or operations of Parent, the Company or their respective Subsidiaries or (ii) accept any other remedy...' The next sentence makes the asymmetry explicit: 'at the written request of Parent, the Company shall... agree to take any action described in the preceding sentence so long as such action is conditioned upon the occurrence of the Closing.' So a divestiture is a Cintas OPTION, exercisable at Cintas's sole election, and UniFirst is contractually gagged from curing its own deal. Section 5.5(a)(iii) -- the reasonable-best-efforts duty to take 'all reasonable steps as may be necessary... to obtain an approval from, or to avoid a Proceeding by, any Governmental Authority' -- is written expressly 'subject to Section 5.5(d),' so the carve-out overrides it. Section 5.5(b) hands Cintas alone the right to 'direct, devise and implement the strategy' for every communication with the FTC, including whether to pull and refile. The bull's stated case is 'this is a clearance-or-remedy case rather than a block case... uniform rental is a route-density business: the overlap is geographic, expressed in laundry plants and delivery routes, and that is exactly what divestitures are built to cure,' with the explicit condition that 'Cintas must be willing to give up whatever plants and routes a remedy requires rather than pay the break fee.' That condition has ZERO contractual support. Cintas is not obliged to divest a single plant or a single route. The G&K precedent is therefore not a floor under the outcome, it is one datapoint about what a buyer with the same walk-away option chose to do in a smaller case -- and in G&K it chose to divest nothing, which is equally consistent with 'Cintas only closes deals it does not have to pay for.' Cintas retains only a duty to DEFEND litigation (5.5(a)(iv)); it has no duty to SETTLE. A 72% completion probability cannot be underwritten off a covenant that lets the buyer decline every available cure.

KILL 2 -- the 'contracted' payout is not contracted, and at Cintas's own 200-day average the spread is exactly zero. The board carries target_px 317.88 and describes it as 'not an estimate; it is arithmetic off contracted terms.' Only $155.00 of that -- 48.8% -- is contracted. The other 51.2% is 0.7720 uncollared Cintas shares, and the fixed ratio is proved by the announcement arithmetic itself (155.00 + 0.7720 x 200.77 = $310.00, the headline price at the 2026-03-09 Cintas close). Live at 2026-07-27: CTAS $210.98 against a 200-day average of $184.55 and a 50-day average of $179.70 -- the buyer is 14.3% above its 200-day and 17.4% above its 50-day, having re-rated on its own 2026-07-15 results. Run the payout at Cintas's 200-day: 155.00 + 0.7720 x 184.552 = $297.47. UniFirst last traded at $297.46. The ENTIRE 6.9% spread is a bet that Cintas sustains a 14% premium to its own 200-day average; it is not compensation for FTC risk at all. At the 50-day average the payout is $293.73 -- BELOW today's UniFirst price, a negative spread before the regulator has done anything. This is a hidden disqualifier the bull names as a condition ('Cintas shares must hold roughly their current level') but never prices: an unhedged buyer is not being paid to take antitrust risk, he is being paid nothing and is short a Cintas mean-reversion put on top.

Against that: a verified floor of $215 or worse. Cintas's own release of 2025-12-22 priced its $275.00 cash proposal as a '64% premium to UniFirst's ninety-day average closing price' as of 2025-12-11, which implies an undisturbed 90-day average of roughly $167.7 -- primary-source confirmation of the board's floor correction and independent proof that the $257.91 figure in general circulation is a post-bid price. UNF's 52-week low is $147.66. So the reward side is zero-to-6.9% and contingent on the BUYER's share price, the risk side is -27.7% to a floor that is if anything generous, and the probability side rests on a covenant that expressly permits the buyer to refuse every remedy. The asymmetry does not survive.
corrections:
(1) MATERIAL, thesis: the 'reasonable best efforts' framing in the bear thesis and dossier UNDERSTATES the problem. It is not merely that there is no hell-or-high-water covenant; Section 5.5(d) is an affirmative carve-out relieving Cintas of any obligation to divest or to accept ANY remedy, overriding the efforts covenant by its own terms, and barring UniFirst from offering a remedy without Cintas's written consent while obliging UniFirst to divest on demand if Cintas asks. Divestiture capacity is a one-way option held by the buyer. The bull's remedy-case pillar fails on this and the dossier's 'Holds up / Does not hold up' table should record it as a documented contractual fact, not an inference from silence.

(2) MATERIAL, numbers: target_px 317.88 is presented as contracted arithmetic. It is 48.8% contracted cash plus 51.2% uncollared buyer equity. Verified live 2026-07-27: CTAS $210.98, 200-day $184.55, 50-day $179.70. Payout at the CTAS 200-day = $297.47, versus UNF at $297.46 -- a zero spread. Payout at the CTAS 50-day = $293.73, a NEGATIVE spread. The dossier's own retraction ('I overstated it a week ago by anchoring on a stale fifty-day average') was wrong to retract: the 50-day is $179.70, the buyer is 17.4% above it, and the point stands. The reward leg of the asymmetry should be restated as a range of roughly -1.3% to +6.9% depending on where Cintas trades, not as a fixed +6.9%.

(3) MINOR, corroboration of the floor (the board's correction is RIGHT and now has a primary source): Cintas's own 2025-12-22 release describes $275.00 as a '64% premium to UniFirst's ninety-day average closing price,' implying an undisturbed ninety-day average near $167.7 as of 2025-12-11. UNF's 52-week low is $147.66. The $215 working floor is therefore charitable, not conservative, and the $257.91 figure carried elsewhere on the board is confirmed to be a post-bid price. No change to downside_floor is required; the confidence in it should rise.

(4) MINOR, in the BULL's favour -- the reverse break fee is real and better-triggered than the bear implies: Section 7.3(b) makes the $350,000,000 Parent Termination Fee payable on termination under Section 7.1(b)(i) (outside date) or 7.1(b)(ii) (permanent antitrust restraint) where the antitrust conditions are the only ones unsatisfied. It does NOT require proving a Cintas breach. Roughly $19.35 per share against 18,083,905 shares (14,532,640 Common + 3,551,265 Class B) is a genuine cushion. Two haircuts the floor should carry: acceptance is an 'irrevocable waiver of any and all claims against the Parent Related Parties, including with respect to the knowing and intentional breach of Parent's obligations... or fraud,' so it is a capped exit price with a full release attached, exactly the shape of an option premium; and on the outside-date route the fee is not collectible until the Termination Date, which under Section 7.1(b)(i) extends AUTOMATICALLY up to two further four-month periods -- to 2027-09-10 -- whenever the unsatisfied condition is the antitrust one. The shares mark to the break price on the day of a complaint; the cash arrives up to fourteen months later, undiscounted in the board's $215.

(5) MATERIAL, floor quality: the standalone parts value of ~$194 rests on revenue and EBITDA the issuer's own controls cannot presently vouch for. UniFirst's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 2026-05-30 (filed 2026-07-08), Item 4, states that the CEO and CFO concluded disclosure controls and procedures 'were not effective,' owing to an unremediated material weakness 'related to our CRM system which affected revenue and receivables as well as a group of legacy applications which affected revenue and receivables, supply inventory and merchandise in service.' Neither the bull, the bear, nor the dossier's red-flag list mentions it. It does not change the direction of the call, but it widens the break-case band downward.

(6) VERIFIED, no correction needed -- all confirmed against primary sources: terms $155.00 cash + 0.7720 CTAS shares (fixed, no collar); signing 2026-03-10; shareholder approval 2026-06-11 (47,458,203 for / 10,251 against / 17,219 abstentions, >99% of votes cast, ~95% of shares); FTC Second Request to BOTH parties 2026-06-11 with the HSR waiting period running 'until 30 days after both Cintas and the Company substantially comply'; no substantial-compliance date disclosed by either party; Termination Date 5:00 p.m. New York time 2027-01-10 with two automatic four-month extensions; Company Termination Fee $213,300,000 and Parent Termination Fee $350,000,000 (defined terms, Article VIII). The catalyst is genuinely LIVE and UNFIRED as of 2026-07-27 -- no FTC complaint, no compliance certification, no clearance, no closing; the most recent event is the Cintas FY26 Q4 release of 2026-07-15 reaffirming a second-half calendar 2026 close. This is not a fired or a soft catalyst. It is a live catalyst whose spread has already been fully harvested (12.1% at announcement to 6.9% today) and whose remaining reward is indistinguishable from a levered long in the buyer's share price.
